paragraphs: What would the girl be like? Beautiful—or not? Dark? Fair? Would she be good-natured? Would she suit the family? My thoughts did not stop with those questions. Why had I suddenly developed this desire for marriage? No, no—was it not that love affair which had exposed me like this before my family? Confused by such thoughts, I reached the bride's house.

As soon as the girl's father introduced himself to me, he cried out in a loud voice, "Mahamayi!" It sounded like an elephant trumpeting. He took some sacred ash from beside his pillow and placed it in my hand, with devotion overflowing. Could I refuse it? I accepted it. I did not apply it.

Even before that I had told my family, "Let seeing the girl wait. Will they agree to a reform marriage? If they will not, what is the use of seeing the girl? It will end just like the first girl I saw!" The bride's family agreed to a reform marriage. Only then came the bride-viewing itself. I felt an embarrassment I cannot describe. However much I tried, my head refused to rise.

At last they made me stand near the passageway and brought the girl to stand some distance away. Many scenes I have seen in life have faded from memory. But that scene remains among those I have never forgotten. Even now, when I think of it, I can see with the same sweetness that enchanting moment at the house on Vilangiamman Temple Street in Chidambaram: she stood standing behind the screen by the kitchen, and for the first time looked at me. It is a scene that does not fade; a scene that cannot be erased.

A wedding date was fixed. On 13 September 1944, I was to meet a new turn in the road of life. In Tiruvarur, my beloved Padma—enthroned in every living cell of my body—and I entered into a life-partner agreement. On the same day, in the same house, my brother-in-law Jayaram was also married. Mine was a Self-Respect marriage ceremony. His was a priestly "vivaha subhamuhurtham."

I cannot fail to mention that Navalar Nedunchezhiyan, today's General Secretary of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, walked nearly six miles from his native village Vadakandam with his younger brother Sezhiyan to attend the wedding. My close friend Ilamvazhuthi, later a party legislator and a distinguished lawyer in Cuddalore, came two days early and worked for the function. Padma and I exchanged garlands under the leadership of the senior Nagapattinam lawyer Vijayaraghavalu.

While our wedding ceremony was still going on, the traditionalists grew anxious that the auspicious lagna fixed for my brother-in-law's wedding might pass. They burst into our ceremony in agitation. They fretted and flared up. So that their lagna should not be missed, we too shifted the speeches connected with our wedding to the evening and gave way to the auspicious hour they so eagerly welcomed.

That night Kalaivanar N. S. Krishnan was to perform his Kinthanar kathakalakshepam. Kalaivanar had changed the very idea that a kathakalakshepam must always carry the musty smell of the old order. Dressed like a distinguished Bhagavata storyteller and seated on stage with accompanying musicians, he would leave the puranic storytellers standing agape, thinking they were about to relish a devotional story dripping with piety.

Then Kalaivanar would thunder: "The Nandan of those days went to the temple; the Kinthan of these days goes to the temple of learning." Faces in the gathering would bloom. "Is this not a feast of ideas!" people would exclaim in delight. His revolutionary kathakalakshepam received welcome, support and praise across the South.

Who could fail to admire Kalaivanar's courage when they saw the story of a young man born in a cheri, living in poverty, going to Madras, receiving an education and proclaiming, "I too am human"? Today we rejoice in a time when the principle "All are equal!" has grown like a banyan tree. But what was the age in which Kalaivanar's Kinthanar revolution took place? What kinds of opposition did those intoxicated with the old order hurl at him?

If that Kinthanar, which had caused such an upheaval, was to be performed at our wedding, could the wedding pavilion contain the crowd? The long, vast pavilion disappeared from sight. A sea of people surged inside. The Kinthanar performance had to be stopped. Hundreds of police came for protection. My brother-in-law and I—the two bridegrooms—could not even enter the pavilion.

At that moment, without my knowing it, my eyes turned toward the women's section. Need I say why? I wanted to see whether she was safe. From within that same crowd, my Padma's eyes too were searching for me with longing and fear. She saw me struggling in the crush. Ah! How her face wilted! Only that morning had the bond of life been tied between us. Where had such affection come from so quickly? Even as I wondered, a great wave rose and separated us so that we could no longer see one another. In that surge, one or two young men broke their legs.

At last the Kinthanar performance was shifted from the pavilion out into the street. Seeing the flood of people, Kalaivanar poured out his ideas that day with fresh vigour. My friends and I, without even eating dinner, sat beside the well in the backyard of the wedding house and listened through the loudspeaker.

There was a way through the backyard to the Kinthanar stage. We decided to go that way and knocked on the back gate. What happened? The women inside immediately began screaming. They thought rough men from the crowd were trying to break down the door. What could we do? Thinking it dangerous to remain there, we ran away. Such was the fate of the bridegroom at his own wedding!

Somehow the wedding events came to an end. Friends and relatives returned to their towns. For about a year, the chapter of married life was one of great happiness. After that, peace of mind began to diminish. Questions arose from every side: "If you keep roaming about without a job like this, where will the future end?" More than all those questions, the arrows of love coming from the one nearest me began to pierce my heart.

The very week after the wedding I had arranged a ten-day tour and gone away to give speeches. I wandered about possessed by party fervour, and no one's words entered my ears. But my wife's advice, without cooling my political zeal, awakened in me a sense of family responsibility. Whenever I had time, I wandered in search of work. Yet I did not want any job that would enslave me. And then—who would give me work?

I began to think intensely: "What is the way to live?" My Padma—what dreams must she have had when she placed the garland around my neck? How disappointed must she be now, seeing my condition! No, no—I must not cause her pain. I made a firm decision. The result? I became an actor.
